sections.h: Paul founds the church at Corinth
sections.b: Paul arrived from Athens about AD 50, lodged and worked with Aquila and Priscilla, and argued in the synagogue every Sabbath (Acts 18:1–4). When opposition grew he moved next door to the house of Titius Justus, and the synagogue leader Crispus believed with his household (Acts 18:7–8). After a vision promising that "a large people in this city belongs to me" (Acts 18:10), Paul stayed eighteen months. The Jewish community accused him before the proconsul Gallio, who refused to hear the case (Acts 18:12–17), and the Delphi inscription naming Gallio dates the scene to about AD 51–52. Paul left from the eastern port of Cenchreae (Acts 18:18); Apollos soon followed him as a teacher there (Acts 18:27–19:1), and Paul later spent three months in Greece, probably in Corinth, where he wrote Romans (Acts 20:2–3).
sections.refs: Acts 18:1–18; Acts 18:27–19:1; Acts 20:2–3; 1 Corinthians 1:14; Romans 16:1; Romans 16:23

common: Most historians accept Luke's outline of Paul's Corinthian stay and date it by the Gallio inscription to about AD 50–52.
uncommon: Some scholars identify Titius Justus (Acts 18:7) with Gaius, Paul's host in Corinth (Romans 16:23).

sections.b: Luke introduces Aquila, a Jew from Pontus, and his wife Priscilla, newly arrived in Corinth after Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2). They shared Paul's trade of tentmaking and his home (Acts 18:3), sailed with him to Ephesus (Acts 18:18–19), and there took the gifted preacher Apollos aside to explain God's way more accurately (Acts 18:26). Priscilla is named first in both of those later scenes, and the Western text and Byzantine copies reverse the order at Acts 18:26, which many scholars see as a later copyist's discomfort with a woman's prominence. Paul's letters show the couple hosting churches in Ephesus and Rome and risking their lives for him (1 Corinthians 16:19; Romans 16:3–5).
sections.refs: Acts 18:2–3; Acts 18:18–19; Acts 18:26; Romans 16:3–5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; 2 Timothy 4:19

common: Priscilla and Aquila were probably already believers when they met Paul, since Luke never describes their conversion.

sections.b: Apollos, an Alexandrian Jew, "a learned speaker and strong in the Scriptures," taught accurately about Jesus at Ephesus though he knew only John's baptism (Acts 18:24–25). Priscilla and Aquila explained God's way to him more accurately, and the Ephesian believers wrote to commend him to the disciples in Achaia, where he argued powerfully from the Scriptures that the Messiah is Jesus (Acts 18:26–28). Luke places him in Corinth when Paul returns to Ephesus (Acts 19:1). Paul's letters confirm his influence there and his good relations with Paul (1 Corinthians 3:4–6; 1 Corinthians 16:12).
sections.refs: Acts 18:24–28; Acts 19:1; 1 Corinthians 1:12; 1 Corinthians 3:4–6; 1 Corinthians 16:12; Titus 3:13

uncommon: Martin Luther suggested that Apollos wrote the Letter to the Hebrews; there is no early evidence for it, but the guess remains popular.

sections.b: Paul stopped briefly at Ephesus on his way to Syria (Acts 18:19–21) and returned to stay more than two years (Acts 19:8–10; Acts 20:31). About twelve disciples of John were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus, and Paul laid hands on them (Acts 19:1–7), and taught three months in the synagogue and two years in the school of Tyrannus, so that "everyone living in Asia heard the Lord's word" (Acts 19:10). The city's fame for magic shows in the failed exorcism of the sons of Sceva and the burning of books worth fifty thousand silver coins (Acts 19:13–19). The riot of the silversmiths, the chant "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" (Acts 19:28), the theater, the Asiarchs and the city's chief clerk (Acts 19:23–41) match what inscriptions show of the city. Paul later called the church's elders to Miletus for his farewell (Acts 20:17–38).

common: The details of the riot (Asiarchs, the clerk of the people, the title "temple warden") are often cited as evidence of Luke's accurate local knowledge.
uncommon: Some scholars think the plural "proconsuls" (Acts 19:38) points to the months after the murder of the proconsul Junius Silanus in AD 54.

sections.b: Paul's question to the disciples at Ephesus, "When you came to believe, did you receive the Holy Spirit?" (Acts 19:2), and the Spirit's coming when he laid hands on them, with tongues and prophecy (Acts 19:6), make this one of the main passages in the debate over a second experience of the Spirit after faith. The KJV's "since ye believed" encouraged that reading; most modern translations have "when you believed." Luke also says Paul set his mind "in the Spirit" to go to Jerusalem (Acts 19:21), went "bound in the Spirit," and was warned by the Holy Spirit in every city (Acts 20:22–23), and that the Holy Spirit made the Ephesian elders overseers (Acts 20:28). The Where Christians differ card at Acts 2:4 sets out the churches' views.

When Paul laid hands on the twelve disciples of John at Ephesus, "They began to speak in tongues and to prophesy" (Acts 19:6). It is the third scene in Acts where a new group receives the Spirit with inspired speech (Acts 2:4; Acts 10:46), a few years before Paul, writing from this same city, discussed tongues and prophecy at length (1 Corinthians 12–14). Pentecostal churches take the scene as part of the pattern for tongues as the first sign of Spirit baptism; others read it as a sign marking a turning point in the spread of the gospel.

sections.h: The disciples of John baptized into Jesus' name
sections.b: At Ephesus Paul met about twelve disciples who had received only "the baptism of John" (Acts 19:3). Paul explained that John's was a baptism of repentance pointing to Jesus, and "they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 19:5), the only clear case in the New Testament of people baptized a second time. Apollos, who also knew only John's baptism, is not said to have been baptized again (Acts 18:25–26). Churches draw different conclusions about rebaptism, and the Oneness Pentecostal practice of baptizing in Jesus' name appeals to this verse (see the card at Acts 19). At Corinth, many "were coming to faith and being baptized" (Acts 18:8).
sections.refs: Acts 19:1–7; Acts 18:8; Acts 18:25–26; Acts 2:38; Acts 8:16; Matthew 28:19

sections.b: Acts shows that John's movement outlived him. Apollos knew only John's baptism (Acts 18:25), and Paul found about twelve disciples at Ephesus, far from the Jordan, who had been baptized "Into the baptism of John" (Acts 19:3). Paul's answer sums up how Luke sees John: "John baptized with a baptism of repentance. He kept telling the people to believe in the one coming after him, that is, in Jesus" (Acts 19:4). Ernst Käsemann thought Luke was absorbing a rival Baptist group into the church; many others read these as believers whose teaching was incomplete.

uncommon: Some scholars think groups devoted to John the Baptist continued for centuries, and see the later Mandaean religion of Iraq and Iran as a distant descendant; most doubt a direct link.

sections.b: Ephesus was famous for magic and for the charms called "Ephesian letters." Luke tells of seven sons of Sceva, Jewish exorcists who tried to use Jesus' name as a formula and were overpowered and stripped by the man they meant to free (Acts 19:13–16). Fear fell on the city; believers came forward "openly admitting and reporting their practices" (Acts 19:18), a phrase that may mean revealing their spells, and those who had practiced magic burned their books in public, worth fifty thousand silver coins (Acts 19:19). Luke sets the scene beside God's real miracles through Paul (Acts 19:11–12), drawing a clear line between God's power and the use of names as magic, as he did with Simon (Acts 8:9–24) and Bar-Jesus (Acts 13:6–12).

sections.h: Gods made by hands at Ephesus
sections.b: Demetrius the silversmith summed up Paul's preaching at Ephesus: "He says that gods produced by hands are not gods" (Acts 19:26), the old teaching of Israel's Scriptures (Psalm 115:4; Isaiah 44:9–20). The craftsmen who made little silver shrines of Artemis feared for their trade, and the city for its goddess and her temple, one of the wonders of the world (Acts 19:24–28). Yet the city's clerk could say that Paul's companions were not temple robbers and had not spoken against the goddess (Acts 19:37): Paul argued against idols without attacking their worshipers.

Paul "summoned the church's elders" from Ephesus to Miletus (Acts 20:17) and told them that the Holy Spirit had placed them in the flock "as overseers, to shepherd the church of God" (Acts 20:28). The same men are called elders (presbyteroi), overseers (episkopoi, the word that became "bishops") and shepherds (pastors), as in Titus 1:5–7 and 1 Peter 5:1–2. The passage is central to the churches' debate about whether bishops are a distinct order above presbyters (see the card at Acts 20). Paul's charge to them is to watch themselves and the flock, to guard against false teachers, and to work and help the weak (Acts 20:28–35).
sections.refs: Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28–35; Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5–7; 1 Peter 5:1–4; Philippians 1:1

common: Most scholars agree that in the first generation "elder" and "overseer" named the same leaders.
uncommon: Some Catholic and Orthodox scholars argue that a single leading overseer existed in some churches from the apostles' time, even while the titles overlapped.

sections.b: On the first day of the week the believers at Troas "had gathered to break bread" (Acts 20:7). After Eutychus was raised, Paul "broke the bread and had something to eat" and talked until dawn (Acts 20:11). Most readers think this was a shared meal that included the Lord's Supper, as Paul describes at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:20–26), and the scene is the earliest clear report of a weekly gathering for it. It is the chief text for churches that celebrate communion every Sunday (see the card at Acts 20).
sections.refs: Acts 20:7–11; Acts 2:42; Acts 2:46; Luke 24:30–35; 1 Corinthians 10:16; 1 Corinthians 11:20–26

sections.h: Synagogue on the Sabbath, church on the first day
sections.b: In Corinth Paul argued in the synagogue "Sabbath after Sabbath" (Acts 18:4), and in Ephesus for three months (Acts 19:8). At Troas the believers met "On the first day of the week" to break bread (Acts 20:7), the earliest clear mention of Christians gathering on that day. Whether the meeting began on Saturday evening (Jewish reckoning) or Sunday evening (Roman reckoning) is debated. The cards at Revelation 1 and Matthew 12 set out the churches' views on the Sabbath and Sunday.

Paul's speech to the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:18–35) is a farewell in the biblical pattern. Like Jacob, Moses, Samuel and Jesus, he looks back on his conduct, claiming he coveted no one's silver or gold (Acts 20:33; compare 1 Samuel 12:3); he looks ahead to suffering (Acts 20:22–25); he hands on his charge (Acts 20:28); and he warns of wolves to come (Acts 20:29–30). It ends with prayer, tears and a final parting (Acts 20:36–38). It is the only speech in Acts that Paul gives to Christians, and the one closest to his letters.
sections.refs: Acts 20:17–38; Genesis 49; Deuteronomy 31–33; 1 Samuel 12:1–5; Luke 22:14–38; John 13–17; 2 Timothy 4:6–8

sections.b: At Ephesus, Priscilla and Aquila heard Apollos, "and they drew him to their side and laid out God's way for him more accurately" (Acts 18:26). Priscilla is named first, and the Western text and Byzantine copies reverse the names, perhaps uneasy at her prominence. Egalitarian readers see a woman teaching theology to a learned man with the Bible's approval; complementarian readers stress that the teaching was private and shared with her husband, and so does not bear on 1 Timothy 2:12. Both agree she was a respected teacher of the faith.

Before sailing from Cenchreae, Paul (or possibly Aquila) had his hair cut short, "for he was keeping a vow" (Acts 18:18). It resembles the Nazirite vow, which ended with the shaving of the dedicated hair at the sanctuary (Numbers 6:18), and later Paul joins four men in completing such vows in the temple (Acts 21:23–26). Luke shows Paul keeping Jewish forms of devotion freely, as he wrote that to the Jews he became as a Jew (1 Corinthians 9:20).

Two officials in this part of Acts refuse to treat the Christians as criminals. Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, dismisses the charge that Paul teaches worship that goes against the law as a dispute over "a word and names" and Jewish law (Acts 18:12–16). At Ephesus the city's chief clerk declares Paul's companions innocent of temple robbery and blasphemy, and warns that the real danger of being accused of an uprising lies with the rioters (Acts 19:35–40). Luke presents these as precedents: the faith is no threat to public order.

sections.h: "I am going to the Gentiles" at Corinth
sections.b: At Corinth Paul shook out his clothes and said to the synagogue, "From now on, I am going to the Gentiles" (Acts 18:6), the second of three such turns in Acts (Acts 13:46; Acts 28:28). Yet he moved only next door, the synagogue leader Crispus believed (Acts 18:8), and in Ephesus he began again in the synagogue (Acts 18:19; Acts 19:8). Scholars such as Jacob Jervell read these turns as local, within a divided Israel; others, such as Jack Sanders, as stages in a final break. The Lord's word that "a large people in this city belongs to me" (Acts 18:10) uses laos, the usual word for Israel, of mostly Gentile believers.

Paul ends his farewell at Miletus by telling the elders to keep in mind the words of the Lord Jesus, "for he himself said, 'Giving is more blessed than receiving'" (Acts 20:35). The saying is in none of the Gospels, though Luke 6:38 and Luke 14:12–14 are close in spirit. It shows that the early church remembered sayings of Jesus beyond those the Gospels record, and it is the best attested of all the agrapha, since it is in the New Testament itself. Joachim Jeremias counted it among the few unwritten sayings with a strong claim to be authentic. Similar maxims circulated among Greeks (Thucydides 2.97), and 1 Clement 2:1 echoes it.
sections.refs: Acts 20:35; Luke 6:38; Luke 14:12–14; 1 Corinthians 7:10; 1 Thessalonians 4:15; 1 Clement 2:1

sections.h: Shepherds of the church of God
sections.b: At Miletus Paul tells the elders that the Holy Spirit has made them overseers "to shepherd the church of God," and warns that "vicious wolves will get in among you and show the flock no mercy" (Acts 20:28–29). The picture joins Ezekiel's judgment on Israel's bad shepherds (Ezekiel 34), Jesus' charge to Peter, "Shepherd my sheep" (John 21:16), and the later word "pastor," Latin for shepherd.

sections.h: Wolves from outside and from within
sections.b: Paul warns the Ephesian elders of two dangers after his departure: "vicious wolves will get in among you" from outside (Acts 20:29), and men from their own group will "say twisted things, so they can pull the disciples away to follow them" (Acts 20:30). The letters to Timothy show false teachers at Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:3–7), and the risen Jesus later praises the Ephesian church for testing those who called themselves apostles and were not (Revelation 2:2).

At Ephesus some of the Asiarchs, "who were on friendly terms with him," warned Paul not to put himself at risk in the theater during the riot (Acts 19:31). Asiarchs were leading men of the province of Asia, connected with its assembly and, many scholars think, with the provincial temples of the emperor. Luke's note that such men were Paul's friends supports his picture of a faith that posed no threat to Rome. Ephesus was also proud of its title "temple warden" (Acts 19:35), later used of its temples to the emperors.

Luke says "God was doing acts of power, and no ordinary ones, through Paul's hands" (Acts 19:11), so that cloths and aprons that had touched his skin healed the sick (Acts 19:12), much as Peter's shadow did (Acts 5:15). At Troas Paul took the fallen Eutychus in his arms and gave him back alive (Acts 20:9–12), as Elijah and Elisha did (1 Kings 17:21; 2 Kings 4:34) and Peter did for Tabitha (Acts 9:36–42). Catholic and Orthodox Christians cite Acts 19:12 for the honor given to relics; many Protestants treat these as signs belonging to the apostolic founding of the church.

Paul tells the Ephesian elders to shepherd "the church of God, which he acquired through his own blood" (Acts 20:28). Read with "God" as the subject, the verse speaks of God's own blood, and Ignatius of Antioch, writing to Ephesus, also speaks of "the blood of God." The fathers explained such language by the unity of Christ's person: what belongs to his human nature can be said of the one who is God. Others read "the blood of his own [Son]." Some manuscripts read "the church of the Lord." The verse is one of the New Testament's key texts for the deity of Christ.

Paul lived and worked with Aquila and Priscilla in Corinth because they shared a craft: "Their craft was making tents" (Acts 18:3). At Miletus he reminded the elders that "these hands met my needs and the needs of the people with me" (Acts 20:34), and he called them to work hard to help the weak (Acts 20:35). Jewish teachers prized a trade alongside the study of Torah (Mishnah Avot 2:2), and Paul refused to be paid by the churches he founded so as to burden no one (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Corinthians 9:12–18).

sections.h: Corinth, Ephesus and the road to Jerusalem (AD 50–57)
sections.b: In Acts 18–20 Paul spends his longest settled years. In Corinth he works as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla, preaches in the synagogue and then next door, and stays eighteen months after a vision of the Lord (Acts 18:1–11); the hearing before Gallio (Acts 18:12–17), dated by the Delphi inscription to about AD 51–52, is the anchor for the chronology of his life. He keeps a vow (Acts 18:18), visits Jerusalem and Antioch, and returns to Ephesus for more than two years of teaching, miracles and conflict (Acts 19). From there he writes 1 Corinthians, and later, from Corinth, Romans. He then travels with delegates from his churches, carrying the collection for Jerusalem (Acts 20:4; Romans 15:25–28), and gives the Ephesian elders at Miletus his only recorded speech to Christians, a farewell that sounds much like his letters (Acts 20:18–35).

sections.h: Gallio and the dates of Paul
sections.b: An inscription at Delphi preserves a letter of Claudius naming Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, dated by Claudius' twenty-sixth acclamation in AD 52. Since proconsuls served one year from early summer, Gallio probably governed from 51 to 52, so Paul's hearing before him (Acts 18:12–17) falls in that year and his eighteen months in Corinth about 50–52. Together with Orosius' date of AD 49 (which he credits to Josephus, though no such passage survives in Josephus) for Claudius' expulsion of the Jews from Rome (Acts 18:2), this is the anchor for nearly every modern chronology of Paul.
